title: How do you make an API audit-proof so EVERY mutation: including FAILED/denied attempts: is traceable to a specific user identity + timestamp + correlation id (centralized audit interceptor writing an immutable/append-only log before and after the action, capturing actor, action, target, outcome), and why must you log the attempt even when authorization fails?
shortTitle: How do you make an API audit-proof so every mutation including failed attempts is traceable
keyPoints: Every audit record captures six fields: actor (from security context), action, target, server-side UTC timestamp, correlation ID, and outcome.
Capture audit centrally with an interceptor or aspect so no endpoint can forget to log.
Log before the action (attempt) and after (outcome) so even a mid-operation crash leaves a trace.
The log store must be immutable and append-only; the application user has INSERT permission only.
Denied attempts must be logged because they are the signal of an attack in progress.
Never log passwords, full card numbers, or tokens; the audit log itself is a high-value target.

s1_definition.oneliner: Log who did what to which target, when, under which correlation ID, and with what outcome, for every mutation including the ones you denied.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Audit record** – captures the actor (who), action (what), target (on what), timestamp (when), correlation ID (which request chain), and outcome (success/failure/denied).
- **Centralized capture** – a Spring interceptor, servlet filter, or AOP aspect so every mutating request flows through the same recording logic automatically.
- **Immutable log** – the store does not allow updates or deletes; the application user has only `INSERT` permission.
- **Before-and-after logging** – the attempt is recorded on arrival, the outcome is recorded after execution, so a crash leaves a trace.
- **Denied attempts** – must be logged because repeated denials are the strongest signal of an attack in progress.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the vault has a security register. Every person who approaches is recorded: not only those allowed in. When Priya tries to open a locker that is not hers and the guard turns her away, that rejected attempt is still written with her name, the time, which locker, and the word "DENIED." An audit-proof API is that register that can never be erased.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Audit Flow:

  Client request
       │
       ▼
  ┌────────────────────────┐
  │  Audit Interceptor     │
  │  1. Record ATTEMPT     │──→  Append-only audit store
  │     (actor, action,    │
  │      target, timestamp,│
  │      correlationId)    │
  └──────────┬─────────────┘
             │
             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────┐
  │  Authorization Check   │
  │  If denied:            │
  │  Record DENIED ────────│──→  Append-only audit store
  │  Return 403            │
  └──────────┬─────────────┘
             │
             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────┐
  │  Service Logic         │
  └──────────┬─────────────┘
             │
             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────┐
  │  Record OUTCOME        │──→  Append-only audit store
  │  (SUCCESS or FAILURE)  │
  └────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An audit-proof API records every state-changing operation and every attempt at one, including denied and failed attempts, in an immutable append-only log. Each record captures six things: the actor from the server-side security context, the action, the target resource, a server-side UTC timestamp, a correlation ID for cross-service tracing, and the outcome. This is implemented centrally with an interceptor so no endpoint can forget to log.

The log is written before the action (the attempt) and after the action (the outcome), so even a mid-operation crash leaves evidence. The store is append-only, meaning the application user has INSERT permission only, and tamper evidence is added by hashing each record with the previous hash, forming a chain.

The reason denied attempts must be logged is that they are the evidence of an attack. At National Bank of India, the fraud team once found nothing during an investigation because the old system logged only successful transfers. An attacker had tried fifty unauthorized transfers, all blocked by authorization, and left zero trace. After the centralized audit interceptor was added, a burst of denials from one identity became a clear alarm.

An audit log is a legal and investigative instrument, not a debug convenience. It never contains passwords, full card numbers, or tokens, because the log itself is a high-value target that must be access-controlled and encrypted.

Remember one sentence: log the attempt even when you deny it, because the attempts you blocked are often more important to record than the ones you allowed.
